question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

To bite one's thumb at someone.
option_1: To bite one's nails anxiously while waiting for news.
option_2: To restrain oneself from saying something hurtful.
option_3: To make a provocative, contemptuous gesture insulting someone.
option_4: To physically confront and fight an opponent.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To make a provocative, contemptuous gesture insulting someone..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "To bite one's thumb at someone" means to make a rude, provocative gesture showing contempt or insult toward someone, historically by flicking the thumbnail from behind the upper teeth. (किसी का तिरस्कार या अपमान करना)
◦ Example: The two rivals stood at opposite ends of the street, each biting his thumb at the other.

 

• This gesture is famously used to provoke a fight in the opening scene of Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet, and it must not be confused with "biting one's tongue", which instead means holding back from speaking.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 confuses the gesture with biting one's nails, a habit linked to nervousness, not contempt.

 

• Option 2 describes "biting one's tongue," the sense of self-restraint, which is the opposite of this openly insulting gesture.

 

• Option 4 wrongly assumes the idiom refers to physical combat itself rather than the insulting gesture that might provoke one.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. A Red-Letter Day – A memorably happy or important day (यादगार दिन)

2. A Slip of the Tongue – An unintentional mistake in speaking (जुबान का फिसलना)

3. A Snake in the Grass – A hidden, treacherous enemy (छिपा हुआ शत्रु)

4. A White Elephant – A costly possession that is more trouble than it is worth (महंगी पर बेकार वस्तु)

5. Add Fuel to the Fire – To make a bad situation worse (आग में घी डालना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

To be an unwanted third person accompanying a couple who wish to be alone together.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Play gooseberry.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Play gooseberry" means being an unwanted third person who accompanies a couple wanting to be alone together.
◦ (किसी जोड़े के साथ अनचाहे तीसरे व्यक्ति के रूप में रहना)

• This idiom is a British colloquial expression and is commonly used when a friend or relative unintentionally intrudes on a couple's romantic time together. (यह मुहावरा तब प्रयोग होता है जब कोई तीसरा व्यक्ति जोड़े के बीच अनावश्यक रूप से आ जाता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Play gooseberry.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: Play devil's advocate (जानबूझकर विपरीत पक्ष रखना): to argue an opposing viewpoint deliberately, just to test an argument, not because one truly believes it.
◦ Example: I don't really disagree with you, I'm just playing devil's advocate to test your reasoning.

• Option 2: Play second fiddle (किसी के अधीन भूमिका निभाना): to take a subordinate or less important role compared to someone else.
◦ Example: The vice-captain often has to play second fiddle to the team captain.

• Option 3: Play to the gallery (सस्ती लोकप्रियता के लिए काम करना): to act in a showy way aimed at winning cheap approval from the least discerning part of an audience.
◦ Example: The politician was accused of playing to the gallery instead of addressing real issues.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. All at Sixes and Sevens – In complete disorder or confusion (पूरी तरह अस्त-व्यस्त)

2. An Old Flame – A former romantic partner (पुराना प्रेमी/प्रेमिका)

3. Apple of Discord – A cause of quarrel or jealousy (झगड़े की जड़)

4. Apple of One's Eye – A cherished, favourite person (आंखों का तारा)

5. At Loggerheads – In sharp disagreement (कड़े मतभेद में)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

I waved and called out to my old friend across the street, but she ______ and walked straight past without a glance.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Cut me dead.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Cut me dead" means to ignore someone completely and deliberately, especially by pretending not to see or recognise them. (मुझे पूरी तरह जानबूझकर अनदेखा करना)
◦ Example: When I met my former business partner at the party, he cut me dead and turned away.

 

• The completed sentence reads: I waved and called out to my old friend across the street, but she cut me dead and walked straight past without a glance. This fits because the sentence describes deliberate, pointed ignoring of someone.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "Cut me short" (to interrupt someone while they are speaking), "Cut me loose" (to release or set someone free from an obligation) and "Cut me some slack" (to be more lenient or less critical toward someone) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them fits the sense of a deliberate, silent snub required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. At the Eleventh Hour – At the very last moment (आखिरी क्षण में)

2. Back to the Wall – In a desperate, defensive situation (मुश्किल हालात में)

3. Bark up the Wrong Tree – To pursue a mistaken course of action (गलत दिशा में प्रयास करना)

4. Beat about the Bush – To avoid getting to the point (घुमा-फिराकर बात करना)

5. Bear the Brunt – To take the main force of something unpleasant (मुख्य आघात सहना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

Break one's duck.
option_1: To fail repeatedly at the same task without improvement.
option_2: To achieve one's first success after a run of failures or a lack of results.
option_3: To end a long streak of good luck abruptly.
option_4: To damage something valuable by accident.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To achieve one's first success after a run of failures or a lack of results..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Break one's duck" means to achieve one's first success after a period of failure or a run of no results, especially a long-awaited first score, goal, or win. (लंबे समय बाद पहली सफलता प्राप्त करना)
◦ Example: The young batsman finally broke his duck with a half-century in the third match.

 

• The idiom originates from cricket, where scoring zero runs is called a "duck"; breaking it means finally getting on the scoreboard, so the phrase applies broadly to any first success after failures, not just cricket.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes continued failure, which is the opposite of finally achieving a first success.

 

• Option 3 wrongly links the idiom to ending good luck, whereas the idiom is specifically about ending a run of failure with success.

 

• Option 4 describes accidental damage, unrelated to the idiom's meaning of achieving a first success.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Bell the Cat – To take on a risky task on others' behalf (जोखिम भरा काम अपने ऊपर लेना)

2. Bite the Bullet – To face a difficult situation with courage (कठिनाई का साहस से सामना करना)

3. Blow One's Own Trumpet – To boast about oneself (अपनी प्रशंसा खुद करना)

4. Bring to Book – To punish or hold accountable (जवाबदेह ठहराना)

5. Burn the Midnight Oil – To work or study late into the night (देर रात तक मेहनत करना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

To sense how a situation or public opinion is developing before deciding how to act.
option_3: Know which way the wind blows
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Know which way the wind blows.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Know which way the wind blows" means sensing how a situation or public opinion is developing before deciding how to act.
◦ (घटनाओं या जनमत की दिशा को पहले से भांप लेना)

• This idiom is a common political and business expression and is commonly used for cautious people who wait to see how things are trending before committing themselves. (यह मुहावरा सतर्क लोगों के लिए प्रयोग होता है जो पहले स्थिति को भांपते हैं)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Know which way the wind blows.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: Read between the lines (गूढ़ार्थ समझना): to understand a hidden or implied meaning that is not directly stated.
◦ Example: If you read between the lines of his email, you'll see he's actually unhappy with the plan.

• Option 2: See eye to eye (सहमत होना): to agree completely with someone on a matter.
◦ Example: The two partners rarely see eye to eye on financial decisions.

• Option 4: Have an axe to grind (स्वार्थ रखना): to have a private, often selfish motive for doing or saying something.
◦ Example: He criticized the policy loudly, but everyone knew he had an axe to grind.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Burning Question – A topic under urgent discussion (ज्वलंत प्रश्न)

2. By and Large – On the whole, generally (सामान्यतः)

3. By Leaps and Bounds – Very rapidly (तेज़ी से)

4. Call a Spade a Spade – To speak frankly and plainly (साफ-साफ कहना)

5. Cast Pearls before Swine – To offer something valuable to those who cannot appreciate it (अयोग्य व्यक्ति को कीमती वस्तु देना)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

Rare items like these sometimes ______ at small, out-of-the-way auctions, much to the delight of bargain hunters.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Go for a song.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Go for a song" means to be sold for a very low price, much less than its real value. (बहुत सस्ते दाम में बिक जाना)
◦ Example: The antique clock went for a song at the yard sale because nobody recognised its value.

 

• The completed sentence reads: Rare items like these sometimes go for a song at small, out-of-the-way auctions, much to the delight of bargain hunters. This fits because the sentence is about items selling for surprisingly little.

 

• The expression is thought to allude to street ballad-sellers of old, who sold printed song-sheets for a trifling sum, so "a song" came to mean a negligible price.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "Go under the hammer" (to be sold at auction, without any implication about the price), "Go through the roof" (to rise very sharply, usually said of prices or tempers) and "Go down in flames" (to fail suddenly and spectacularly) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them specifically conveys the sense of a very low selling price required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Castle in the Air – An impractical, unrealistic plan (हवाई किला)

2. Cock a Snook – To show open disrespect or defiance (खुलेआम अनादर दिखाना)

3. Cold Shoulder – Deliberately unfriendly treatment (उपेक्षापूर्ण व्यवहार)

4. Cry Wolf – To raise a false alarm (झूठी चेतावनी देना)

5. Cut and Dried – Fixed and settled beforehand (पहले से तय)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

Not to mince matters.
option_1: To speak frankly and directly, without softening unpleasant truths.
option_2: To avoid discussing a difficult topic altogether.
option_3: To chop information into very small, manageable pieces.
option_4: To exaggerate a story to make it sound worse than it is.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To speak frankly and directly, without softening unpleasant truths..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Not to mince matters" means to speak plainly and directly, without softening unpleasant truths or being diplomatic. (बिना लाग-लपेट के सीधी बात कहना)
◦ Example: Not to mince matters, the manager told the team that their performance had been unacceptable.

 

• The word "mince" literally means to chop something into tiny pieces, so the idiom pictures someone refusing to soften or dress up a harsh truth before delivering it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 wrongly suggests avoidance of the topic, whereas the idiom actually means addressing it directly and honestly.

 

• Option 3 takes the word "mince" too literally, applying its cooking sense of chopping food rather than its figurative sense of softening speech.

 

• Option 4 confuses plain speaking with exaggeration; the idiom is about honesty, not overstatement.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Dark Horse – An unexpected candidate who surprises everyone (अप्रत्याशित विजेता)

2. Draw a Blank – To fail to get any result (कोई परिणाम न मिलना)

3. Eat Humble Pie – To apologize and accept humiliation (माफी मांगकर अपमान सहना)

4. Face the Music – To accept the unpleasant consequences of one's actions (परिणाम भुगतना)

5. Fight Tooth and Nail – To fight fiercely and with all one's strength (पूरी ताकत से लड़ना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

To act with reckless abandon, ignoring caution or the consequences of one's actions.
option_2: Throw one's cap over the windmill
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Throw one's cap over the windmill.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Throw one's cap over the windmill" means acting with reckless abandon, ignoring caution or the consequences of one's actions.
◦ (बिना परिणामों की परवाह किए लापरवाही से काम करना)

• This idiom is a literary, somewhat old-fashioned expression and is commonly used to describe someone who abandons prudence for a bold, impulsive act. (यह मुहावरा सावधानी छोड़कर साहसिक कार्य करने के लिए प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Throw one's cap over the windmill.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: Sit on the fence (तटस्थ रहना): to avoid taking a clear position or making a decision on an issue.
◦ Example: The senator sat on the fence for weeks before finally voting on the bill.

• Option 3: Keep one's powder dry (सही अवसर के लिए तैयार रहना): to stay prepared and wait patiently for the right moment to act.
◦ Example: Investors were told to keep their powder dry until the market stabilised.

• Option 4: Hedge one's bets (जोखिम कम करने के उपाय करना): to reduce risk by supporting more than one possible outcome.
◦ Example: She hedged her bets by applying to several universities at once.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Fish in Troubled Waters – To take advantage of a chaotic situation (अशांति का लाभ उठाना)

2. Foot the Bill – To pay the cost of something (खर्च वहन करना)

3. Get Cold Feet – To lose one's nerve before doing something (हिम्मत खो देना)

4. Get the Sack – To be dismissed from a job (नौकरी से निकाला जाना)

5. Give a Piece of One's Mind – To scold someone frankly (कड़ी फटकार लगाना)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

The detective realized that the mysterious letter was just a ______, meant to distract him from the real suspect.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Red herring.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Red herring" means a false or misleading clue deliberately introduced to distract attention from the real issue. (ध्यान भटकाने वाला झूठा सुराग)
◦ Example: The subplot about the missing necklace turned out to be a red herring in the mystery novel.

 

• The completed sentence reads: The detective realized that the mysterious letter was just a red herring, meant to distract him from the real suspect. This fits because the sentence describes a deliberately misleading clue.

 

• The expression is thought to come from the old practice of dragging a smoked (red) herring across a trail to throw hunting dogs off the scent.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "Shot in the dark" (a guess made with little or no information to go on), "Wild goose chase" (a hopeless and futile search or pursuit) and "Storm in a teacup" (a great deal of fuss over something unimportant) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them specifically conveys a deliberately planted false clue as required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Go through Fire and Water – To face great danger or hardship (भारी कठिनाइयों का सामना करना)

2. Green with Envy – Extremely jealous (ईर्ष्या से भर जाना)

3. Hang by a Thread – To be in a very precarious situation (बहुत नाजुक स्थिति में होना)

4. Hard Nut to Crack – A very difficult problem or person (कठिन समस्या या व्यक्ति)

5. Have a Bee in One's Bonnet – To be obsessed with an idea (किसी विचार से ग्रस्त रहना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

At sea.
option_1: Completely confident and in control of a situation.
option_2: Currently traveling by ship on a voyage.
option_3: Sharing the same difficult situation as other people.
option_4: Feeling confused, bewildered, and unsure what to do next.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Feeling confused, bewildered, and unsure what to do next..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "At sea" means feeling confused, bewildered, or completely unsure what to do. (उलझन में या हैरान-परेशान होना)
◦ Example: When the new software was installed without any training, most employees were completely at sea.

 

• The idiom is often used with "completely" or "all" for emphasis, as in "all at sea," and should not be confused with "in the same boat," which means sharing someone else's difficulty rather than simply feeling lost.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes confidence and control, which is the opposite of the confusion the idiom expresses.

 

• Option 2 takes the phrase literally, as if it referred to an actual sea voyage rather than a mental state.

 

• Option 3 confuses the idiom with "in the same boat," which is about sharing a predicament with others, not about feeling confused.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Hit the Nail on the Head – To describe exactly what is causing a situation (सही बात कहना)

2. In the Doldrums – In a state of inactivity or low spirits (उदासी की स्थिति में)

3. In the Limelight – Being the focus of public attention (चर्चा में होना)

4. Iron in the Fire – A plan or project currently in progress (चल रही योजना)

5. Keep One's Fingers Crossed – To hope for a good outcome (शुभकामना के लिए आशा रखना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

To solve a complex or seemingly impossible problem in a swift, decisive way.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Cut the Gordian knot.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Cut the Gordian knot" means to solve a complex or seemingly impossible problem in a bold, decisive manner.
◦ (किसी जटिल समस्या को साहसिक और निर्णायक ढंग से हल करना)

• This idiom is a classic exam idiom rooted in Greek legend and is commonly used to describe bold, unconventional solutions to problems others consider unsolvable. (यह मुहावरा एक प्रसिद्ध यूनानी कथा से जुड़ा है और साहसिक व अपरंपरागत समाधान के लिए प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Cut the Gordian knot.

 

Additional Information

• Option 2: Bite the bullet (दर्द या कठिनाई सहते हुए किसी काम को करने का साहस करना): to face a painful or difficult situation with courage and get it over with.
◦ Example: She decided to bite the bullet and confront her boss about the pay cut.

• Option 3: Beat around the bush (मुद्दे की बात से बचना, घुमा-फिराकर बात करना): to avoid talking directly about the main issue.
◦ Example: Stop beating around the bush and tell me what really happened.

• Option 4: Throw in the towel (हार मान लेना): to give up on a task or contest, admitting defeat.
◦ Example: After three failed attempts, he finally threw in the towel and quit the project.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. A Bad Patch – Difficult period (कठिन समय)

2. A Bolt from the Blue – A sudden shock (अचानक झटका)

3. A Close Shave – A narrow escape (बाल-बाल बचना)

4. A Cock and Bull Story – An unbelievable story (मनगढ़ंत कहानी)

5. A Drop in the Ocean – A very small amount compared to what is needed (ऊंट के मुंह में जीरा)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

Even after being reassured many times, my uncle continues to ______ about the losses he suffered in the stock market ten years ago.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Harp on the same string.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Harp on the same string" means to keep repeating the same point or complaint over and over again, often to the point of irritation. (बार-बार एक ही बात दोहराना)
◦ Example: My grandmother keeps harping on the same string about how children today don't respect their elders.

 

• The completed sentence reads: Even after being reassured many times, my uncle continues to harp on the same string about the losses he suffered in the stock market ten years ago. This fits because he keeps returning to the same old complaint instead of moving on.

 

• The expression comes from the image of a musician who keeps striking the same string of an instrument repeatedly instead of playing a full tune, producing a monotonous, repetitive sound.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "beat about the bush" (to avoid speaking directly about an issue), "cry over spilt milk" (to regret something that has already happened and cannot be changed) and "let bygones be bygones" (to forgive and forget past disputes) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them fits the sense of habitual, repetitive complaining required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

6. A Fish Out of Water – Uncomfortable in unfamiliar surroundings (अनजान माहौल में असहज)

7. A Leopard Cannot Change Its Spots – People cannot change their basic nature (स्वभाव नहीं बदलता)

8. A Piece of Cake – Something very easy (बहुत आसान काम)

9. A Red-Letter Day – A memorable, happy day (यादगार दिन)

10. A Storm in a Teacup – Great fuss over a trivial matter (राई का पहाड़ बनाना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

To writing on the wall.
option_1: An artistic decoration used to brighten up a dull wall.
option_2: A message left behind for someone before departing on a journey.
option_3: An unmistakable indication that failure or disaster is imminent.
option_4: An official public notice announcing government policy.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. An unmistakable indication that failure or disaster is imminent..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "To writing on the wall" means an unmistakable sign that something unpleasant or disastrous is about to happen, especially the end or downfall of something. (दीवार पर लिखी इबारत – आसन्न विनाश का स्पष्ट संकेत)
◦ Example: When the company's biggest client left, employees could see the writing on the wall and started looking for new jobs.

 

• The phrase carries a strong sense of inevitability — it is used only for warnings that are ignored at one's own peril, not for ordinary predictions or casual advice.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 treats the phrase literally, as if it referred to actual decorative text painted on a wall, rather than a figurative warning.

 

• Option 2 confuses the idiom with the unrelated idea of leaving a note or message before departing, which has nothing to do with impending doom.

 

• Option 4 mistakes the idiom for a literal government notice or public announcement, ignoring its figurative sense of foreboding.

 

5 Important Idioms

11. Add Fuel to the Fire – To worsen a situation (आग में घी डालना)

12. All Ears – Listening attentively (पूरा ध्यान देकर सुनना)

13. All Thumbs – Clumsy (अनाड़ी/फूहड़)

14. An Axe to Grind – A hidden personal motive (निजी स्वार्थ)

15. Apple of Discord – A cause of dispute (झगड़े का कारण)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

To reach a peak of quality or popularity and then begin an irreversible decline, often by resorting to a gimmick that signals the beginning of the end.
option_1: Ride on the crest of the wave
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Jump the shark.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Jump the shark" means to reach the highest point of popularity or quality and then begin a noticeable, often irreversible decline.
◦ (अपने शिखर पर पहुंचकर गिरावट की शुरुआत करना)

• This idiom is a modern, informal expression born from television criticism and is commonly used for TV shows, brands, or careers that introduce a desperate gimmick once their best days are behind them. (यह एक आधुनिक बोलचाल का मुहावरा है, जो टीवी शो, ब्रांड या करियर के पतन के लिए प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Jump the shark.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: Ride on the crest of the wave (सफलता के शिखर पर होना): to be at the very height of success or popularity.
◦ Example: The band was riding on the crest of the wave after their album topped the charts worldwide.

• Option 2: Have one's day (अपना स्वर्णिम समय बिताना): to enjoy a period of success, fame, or influence.
◦ Example: Every dog has its day, and this small startup finally had its day when it went public.

• Option 3: Be over the moon (बहुत खुश होना): to be extremely happy or delighted about something.
◦ Example: She was over the moon when she heard she had topped the merit list.

 

5 Important Idioms

16. At Daggers Drawn – In extreme hostility (कट्टर शत्रुता में)

17. At Sixes and Sevens – In confusion (अस्त-व्यस्त/भ्रम में)

18. Back to the Drawing Board – Start over after failure (नए सिरे से शुरुआत करना)

19. Bark Up the Wrong Tree – Pursue a mistaken course (गलत दिशा में प्रयास करना)

20. Bear the Brunt – To face the worst of something (सबसे बुरा परिणाम भुगतना)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

I'm afraid fixing computer hardware is ______; you should ask someone from the IT department instead.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Not in my line.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Not in my line" means something that does not fall within one's own field, profession, or area of expertise, and is used to politely decline a task one is unqualified for. (मेरे क्षेत्र या दक्षता के बाहर होना)
◦ Example: Repairing electrical wiring is not in my line — you should call a qualified electrician.

 

• The completed sentence reads: I'm afraid fixing computer hardware is not in my line; you should ask someone from the IT department instead. The phrase fits because the speaker is admitting the task lies outside their expertise.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "not in my shade", "not in my size" and "not in my tune" — are not established English idioms at all. Each has been formed by simply replacing "line" with an unrelated noun, and none of them carries any accepted meaning in English.

 

5 Important Idioms

21. Beat a Hasty Retreat – Withdraw quickly (जल्दी से पीछे हटना)

22. Behind Closed Doors – In private, secretly (गुप्त रूप से)

23. Beyond the Pale – Unacceptable behaviour (अस्वीकार्य व्यवहार)

24. Bird's Eye View – A general overview (सामान्य विहंगम दृष्टि)

25. Bite Off More Than One Can Chew – Take on more than one can manage (क्षमता से अधिक काम लेना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

Kicked up a row.
option_1: Organized a friendly gathering for neighbours.
option_2: Created a noisy disturbance or angry scene in public.
option_3: Rowed a boat vigorously across a river.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Created a noisy disturbance or angry scene in public..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Kicked up a row" means to create a loud disturbance, quarrel, or angry scene, usually in public or in front of others. (हंगामा या झगड़ा खड़ा करना)
◦ Example: The passenger kicked up a row at the airport counter when his flight was cancelled.

 

• Here, "row" is pronounced to rhyme with "cow" and means a noisy quarrel — a completely different word from the identically spelled "row" meaning a straight line or the act of rowing a boat.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 misreads "row" as a row of houses or a street, turning the idiom into something about neighbourly gatherings rather than a disturbance.

 

• Option 3 confuses "row" (a quarrel) with the unrelated verb "row", meaning to propel a boat with oars.

 

• Option 4 reverses the actual meaning — the idiom describes stirring up conflict, not calmly settling one.

 

5 Important Idioms

26. Bite the Dust – To fail or die (असफल होना/मरना)

27. Blow One's Own Trumpet – To boast (अपनी प्रशंसा स्वयं करना)

28. Blow Hot and Cold – To be inconsistent (अस्थिर रवैया रखना)

29. Break the Ice – To initiate conversation in an awkward setting (बातचीत शुरू करना)

30. Bring to Book – To punish or hold accountable (जवाबदेह ठहराना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

Remaining neutral or undecided on an issue, deliberately avoiding taking a clear side.
option_4: Draw a line in the sand
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Sitting on the fence.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Sitting on the fence" means to avoid making a decision or taking sides in a dispute or debate.
◦ (किसी मुद्दे पर तटस्थ रहना, निर्णय न लेना)

• This idiom is a classic exam idiom often used in political and social contexts and is commonly used to criticise people who refuse to commit to either side of an argument. (यह मुहावरा प्रायः राजनीतिक व सामाजिक संदर्भों में तटस्थ रहने वालों की आलोचना हेतु प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Sitting on the fence.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: Burn one's bridges (वापसी का सारा रास्ता बंद कर देना): to act in a way that destroys any possibility of returning to a previous situation.
◦ Example: By insulting his old employer publicly, he burned his bridges for good.

• Option 2: Toe the line (नियमों का पालन करना): to conform strictly to a rule, standard, or expectation set by an authority.
◦ Example: New recruits are expected to toe the line during their probation period.

• Option 4: Draw a line in the sand (स्पष्ट सीमा तय करना): to set a firm limit beyond which one will not go, taking a clear, decisive stand.
◦ Example: The union drew a line in the sand and refused to accept any further pay cuts.

 

5 Important Idioms

35. Call a Spade a Spade – To speak plainly and honestly (साफ-साफ कहना)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

Overcome with guilt, the boy finally decided to go to his parents and ______ about the broken vase.
option_1: Make a clean chest of it
option_2: Make a fair breast of it
option_3: Make a clean shoulder of it
option_4: Make a clean breast of it
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Make a clean breast of it.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Make a clean breast of it" means to confess something fully and honestly, especially something one feels guilty about, holding nothing back. (पूरी बात खुलकर और ईमानदारी से कबूल करना)
◦ Example: After weeks of guilt, she decided to make a clean breast of it and told her friend the truth about the accident.

 

• The completed sentence reads: Overcome with guilt, the boy finally decided to go to his parents and make a clean breast of it about the broken vase. This fits perfectly because he is choosing to confess honestly rather than hide his mistake.

 

• The expression comes from the old image of baring one's chest ("breast") as a gesture of openness and sincerity, symbolising that nothing is being hidden.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "make a clean chest of it", "make a fair breast of it" and "make a clean shoulder of it" — are not established English idioms at all. Each has been formed by simply replacing a key word in the genuine phrase "make a clean breast of it" with a similar-sounding term, and none of them carries any accepted meaning in English.

 

5 Important Idioms

36. Cast Pearls Before Swine – To offer something valuable to those who do not appreciate it (अयोग्य व्यक्ति को कीमती चीज़ देना)

37. Cast a Slur – To defame someone (बदनाम करना)

38. Castles in the Air – Unrealistic plans or daydreams (हवाई किले बनाना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

Rising to the occasion.
option_1: Meeting the demands of a difficult situation with unexpectedly strong performance.
option_2: Standing up out of respect when someone important enters a room.
option_3: Postponing an important event to a more convenient date.
option_4: Losing composure and panicking when faced with a crisis.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Meeting the demands of a difficult situation with unexpectedly strong performance..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Rising to the occasion" means to perform exceptionally well precisely when a situation demands it, especially under pressure or in a crisis. (अवसर के अनुरूप असाधारण प्रदर्शन करना)
◦ Example: Though she had never spoken publicly before, the young manager rose to the occasion and delivered a brilliant presentation.

 

• The key sense lies in "rising" — it signals a person lifting their performance above their normal level to match the seriousness of the moment, not a physical or literal act of standing up.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 takes "rising" literally, as the physical act of standing up out of courtesy, which is unrelated to the idiom's figurative meaning.

 

• Option 3 confuses the idiom with postponing or rescheduling an event, which has nothing to do with performing well under pressure.

 

• Option 4 reverses the actual meaning — the idiom describes excelling under pressure, not losing control of oneself.

 

5 Important Idioms

41. Cool One's Heels – To wait for a long time (लंबे समय तक इंतजार करना)

42. Cry Over Spilt Milk – To lament something that cannot be undone (बीती बात पर पछताना)

43. Cry Wolf – To raise a false alarm (झूठी चेतावनी देना)

44. Cut a Sorry Figure – To look foolish or pitiable (हास्यास्पद स्थिति में पड़ना)

45. Dark Horse – Someone unexpectedly successful (अप्रत्याशित सफल व्यक्ति)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

In the very early or developing stage of something, before it has fully grown or become established.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. In the bud.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "In the bud" means at an early, undeveloped stage — before something has had the chance to grow or mature fully.
◦ (प्रारंभिक या विकासशील अवस्था में)

• This idiom is a horticultural metaphor and is commonly used together with verbs like "nip" to describe stopping a problem before it can develop further. (यह मुहावरा पौधों की कली से जुड़ा रूपक है, जो किसी समस्या को शुरुआत में ही रोकने के संदर्भ में प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. In the bud.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: From scratch (शून्य से, बिना किसी पूर्व सहायता के शुरू करना): starting something completely anew, without using anything already prepared.
◦ Example: After the fire destroyed his shop, he had to build his business from scratch.

• Option 3: Once in a blue moon (कभी-कभार, बहुत कम): something that happens very rarely.
◦ Example: My cousin lives abroad, so we meet only once in a blue moon.

• Option 4: In the nick of time (ऐन वक्त पर): at the last possible moment, just before it is too late.
◦ Example: The doctor arrived in the nick of time to save the patient's life.

50. Fair and Square – Honest and just (ईमानदारी से)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

Furious at his betrayal of the group's trust, his friends unanimously decided ______, and for months afterward not a single person spoke to him.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To send to Coventry.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "To send to Coventry" means to deliberately exclude someone from a group and refuse to speak or associate with them, as a form of punishment or disapproval. (जानबूझकर किसी का सामाजिक बहिष्कार करना)
◦ Example: When he broke the team's trust, the players decided to send him to Coventry for the rest of the season.

 

• The completed sentence reads: Furious at his betrayal of the group's trust, his friends unanimously decided to send to Coventry, and for months afterward not a single person spoke to him. The phrase fits because it describes a collective, deliberate act of social ostracism.

 

• The expression comes from the English Civil War era, when Royalist soldiers captured by Parliamentarians were reportedly sent to the town of Coventry, a Parliamentarian stronghold, where the local residents refused to associate with them.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "to turn a blind eye" (to deliberately ignore something one knows is wrong), "to break the ice" (to ease tension and start a conversation in an awkward situation) and "to bury the hatchet" (to end a quarrel and make peace) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them fits the sense of deliberate social ostracism required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

51. Feather in One's Cap – An achievement to be proud of (गर्व की बात/उपलब्धि)

52. Fight Tooth and Nail – To fight fiercely (पूरी ताकत से लड़ना)

53. Fish in Troubled Waters – To take advantage of a chaotic situation (अशांति का फायदा उठाना)

54. Flog a Dead Horse – To waste effort on a hopeless cause (व्यर्थ प्रयास करना)

55. Get Cold Feet – To lose courage before doing something (हिम्मत हार जाना)
